title: 'Not a failure': Lazaro defends missed ASEAN sea code deadline
summary: Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro says negotiators could have finished the long-delayed agreement with another five to six months.

blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 7:08pm

MANILA, Philippines — Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said the Philippines' inability to shepherd ASEAN to a final South China Sea code of conduct during its chairship was "not a failure," as negotiators had already settled about 80% of the draft text.
"We have done 80% or more than that. So I don't think it's a failure," Lazaro told reporters during her end-of-day briefing on the second day of the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila.

She said negotiators could have finished the text with another five to six months, but "we have to stop and give it to the next chair" — Singapore, which takes over the 11-member bloc's rotating chairship in 2027.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has been vocal about the government's aspiration of wrapping up all negotiations for the code during its term as ASEAN chair. Negotiators from ASEAN and China met monthly from January to speed up the talks, and as recently as July, Lazaro said the parties had the "political will" to finish by year-end.
Asked whether Manila was disappointed after Marcos' earlier optimism on completing the code this year, Lazaro said: "Why would we be frustrated? We just needed more time."

But prior to 2026, decades of delay in finalizing the code have already frustrated the bloc, as technically ASEAN and China have been sitting on the issue for more than two decades since signing the non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea in 2002.

On Sunday, after the end of the first day of the summit, Lazaro said three of four "milestone" issues about the code remained unresolved, including whether the code would be legally binding, which Beijing has long objected to.

The code is meant to set practical rules of behavior to manage tensions in a waterway that China claims almost entirely, overlapping with the claims of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan.

A 2016 arbitral ruling found that China's sweeping claims had no basis in international law, a decision Beijing rejects. Meanwhile, Manila has repeatedly accused Chinese coast guard vessels of firing water cannon and making dangerous maneuvers against Philippine ships near Ayungin Shoal and Scarborough Shoal, while Beijing says its actions have been lawful and professional.
Lazaro declined on Monday to set a new target and stressed that negotiations for the code would now be shepherded by Singapore next year.

"I don't think I can give you a timeline as to when the COC will finish," she said, adding that she was confident Singapore could complete the work when it starts next year. She noted that ASEAN's coordinator for relations with China, which co-chairs the talks with Beijing, will also change from Malaysia to Laos by mid-2027.

The DFA chief also defended the remarks by Chinese Premier Li Qiang at the ASEAN-China summit, where he reaffirmed Beijing's commitment to an effective and substantive code consistent with the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Lazaro was asked to comment on whether such a statement appeared to be "lip service" as it is nearly identical to past Chinese statements.
The DFA chief said the language reflected a standing commitment that ASEAN leaders had also repeated, and that any change to it would draw attention.
Asked whether confrontations between Chinese and Philippine vessels would ease once a code is in place, Lazaro said: "I don't think I can speculate."

Lazaro also sidestepped a question on whether concerns were raised over the police dispersal of protesters near the summit, saying ASEAN leaders discussed regional issues and "no one from the Philippine delegation is talking about anything domestic."

Police clashed on Sunday with activists at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila as they tried to march toward the summit venue at the Philippine International Convention Center to protest US President Donald Trump's visit and the Pax Silica initiative. Labor group Kilusang Mayo Uno and other progressive organizations that led the demonstrations have called the dispersal violent.

Lazaro declined to discuss Trump's visit, including whether Manila and Washington would sign the framework agreement for the US-led Pax Silica initiative, saying her briefing covered only the day's meetings.
Trump is due to arrive on Tuesday for a special meeting with ASEAN leaders.
